[Getting started](/auth/start/getting-started/) ends with a server that signs people in. This guide adds what it left out: configuration read and checked at startup, the client IP behind a proxy, the CSRF token layer, email verification, password reset and a session-aware route. The same pieces, with an end-to-end test, are in `examples/basic` in the repository.

The server is six files. Install and the Prisma schema are the same as in Getting started.

## Configuration

Read every setting once, at startup, and fail before the server listens. The two secrets must differ: the auth secret derives the keys for codes and device cookies, the CSRF secret signs CSRF tokens only.

<Code code={configTs} lang="ts" title="src/config.ts" />

`TRUST_PROXY` is the number of reverse proxies in front of the server. Every per-IP limit and audit row reads the client IP, and `X-Forwarded-For` is written by the client up to the first proxy you run, so the server trusts exactly that many hops from the right. Trusting everything lets a client choose its own rate-limit bucket; trusting nothing behind a proxy puts every client in one bucket, where one attacker blocks logins for everyone. `parseTrustProxy` refuses `true` for that reason.

<Code code={dbTs} lang="ts" title="src/db.ts" />

## Auth

<Code code={authTs} lang="ts" title="src/auth.ts" />

- **One TTL in two places.** The Redis store guards a user's revocation epoch for `maxSessionTtl`, and `createAuth` refuses a session that could outlive it. Keeping `rememberMeTtl` and `maxSessionTtl` in one constant makes the pair impossible to get out of step.
- **`noeviction`.** Run this Redis with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. Under an evicting policy Redis may drop an epoch, which signs users out, a lockout counter, which hands an attacker a fresh budget, or a lock key, which ends a lock early. With `noeviction` a full Redis refuses writes and the flows fail closed.
- **A logger.** Without one, the package's warnings (a breach check that could not run, a mailer that threw) go nowhere.
- **The mailer is a parameter** so the server can pass a development mailer and production a queue; see [Mail into your templates and queue](/auth/build/mail/).

## CSRF

The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, which stops most cross-site requests on its own. This module adds the three checks [CSRF](/auth/learn/csrf/) describes, for every unsafe method:

1. the `Origin` header must be the app's own;
2. `Sec-Fetch-Site` must say `same-origin` whenever the browser sends it;
3. a signed double-submit token: the page reads the `csrf` cookie and echoes it in an `X-CSRF-Token` header, and the token's HMAC binds it to the current session, or, before sign-in, to a random id this browser alone holds in an HttpOnly cookie.

<Code code={csrfTs} lang="ts" title="src/csrf.ts" />

Every change of session changes the binding, so the server hands out a new token whenever it sets a session cookie and when it signs out.

## Responses

The flows return `AuthResult` values. A refusal has a public `code` and an internal `reason`; only `toPublicError(result)` goes over the wire, because the reason can tell a wrong password from an unknown account.

<Code code={httpTs} lang="ts" title="src/http.ts" />

## Routes

<Code code={serverTs} lang="ts" title="src/server.ts" />

- **One validation per request.** `validateRequest` checks the session, slides its idle timeout (at most one write a minute) and refuses a revoked one. Pass `touch: false` for traffic the client makes on its own, such as polls, so they do not keep a session alive.
- **Answers that reveal nothing.** Register and the reset request answer `202` whatever the address. The reset request does no per-account work on the response path: the lookup and the mail run in a job, detached in-process here, on your queue once you set `passwordReset.enqueue`.
- **The reset link** points at `/reset-password#<token>`. The fragment never reaches a server log or a `Referer`; the page reads it and posts it with the new password. A completed reset revokes every session and lifts a lockout.
- **Verification can rotate the session**, because verifying an address signs out the account's other sessions; when it does, the response carries the new session cookie and a new CSRF token.
- **Sign-in sets the device cookie** (`__Host-device`) beside the session. It matters only while the account is locked, where it lets the owner's correct password through; see [Brute force and lockout](/auth/learn/brute-force-and-lockout/).

## Before going live

- Serve over HTTPS and leave `session.cookie.secure` on (it is on whenever `NODE_ENV` is `production` here).
- Set `TRUST_PROXY` to the number of proxies you actually run.
- Point the mailer at a queue.
- Add an `audit` sink if you need a record of sign-ins and refusals.
- Delete expired tokens now and then (`expiresAt` is indexed): `prisma.authToken.deleteMany({ where: { expiresAt: { lt: new Date() } } })`.
